questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were so many. First of all, the good reputation of UC Berkeley and its program in Environmental Economics and Policy, a field which few universities offer enough courses in. Secondly, I have family in the Bay Area. Third, the nature in California and neighbouring states is incredible. Fourth, the US is a very diverse place, and the Bay Area in particular is quite progressive and interesting culturally.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved my time at UCB!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty straightforward. The CalCentral portal tells you everything you need to know.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was international student orientation and then the Golden Bear Orientation during the first couple days which gives students every opportunity to have all their questions answered and a chance to meet fellow students, both American and internationals.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It was kind of fun (depends a lot on your orientation leaders) but also too expensive and a lot of the information was actually unnecessary.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Apartments, co-ops, dorms. Altough note that the term 'on campus' in Berkeley is not literally on campus but rather on the periphery of campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: It is possible to buy meal plans and use the many dining halls around campus, but it's expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would recommend the co ops! They are by far the cheapest accomodation option, relatively easy to get into, include as much organic food as you can eat and allows you to meet a lot of American and international students from day one. No matter where you live in Berkeley, though, be prepared to share a room. It is very rare to get a single as a newcomer.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's generally very expensive and there's a lot of uncertainty when trying to find housing from abroad. The co ops are great but can also be dirty and challenging to live in for Danish exchange students, especially if you are not open to cooperative living. That being said, try the co ops anyway!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't remember so it must have been very easy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The international student office is always there to help if you need it. UCB generally has a lot of student resources.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful, although I didn't get a music class I wanted. Be prepared to change your schedule last minute and be patient. At UCB you can drop classes until the third week of the semester, so sometimes spots in  classes that are initially full open up at the start of the semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Go with the flow, find information on CalCentral and ask for help from international student office or fellow students if you need it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was an appropriate level, I think. Not necessarily higher academic level than at KU, but there is so much to choose from and it's much easier to mix and match courses at UCB than at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There are maybe less lecture and lab hours (especially if you're a Science student at KU) but more small assignments, so you have to stay on top of those. The grades are usually based on many different aspects (e.g., attendance, homework, midterm, final exam), so don't expect to get good grades if you only prioritize the final exam (which you can get away with at KU).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
International Environmental Economics (ENVECON C132)
CLIMATE JUSTICE (ENERES C160)
Philosophy of Science (PHILOS 128)
Foundations of Data Science (DATA C8)

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer:
Supervised Independent Study and Research (ENVECON 199)
Economics of Water Resources (ENVECON 162)
Data Science for Economists (ECON 148)
Advanced Chinese (CHINESE 100B)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you want to get an introduction to python, do one of the introductory data science or computer science courses at UCB, they're all generally really good and well-structured. All my courses were good except ENVECON 162, which was bad not because of the material but because of the professor.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Just be prepared for 'the land of the fee'. Remember, sales taxes are never included on the price tag but added when you pay.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: GBO was unexpectedly expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: JOIN JOIN JOIN a club or student organization or something like that, it's the best way to feel belonging at a new school, and UCB has SOOOO many different clubs and activities to join for all and any interests.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: ALL KINDS OF CLUBS: sports, music, politics, magazines, radio, film, major-specific, gender, origami, outdoor, ethnic groups, furry club, (academic) sororities and fraternities, food clubs, you name it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do what you like, there's something for everyone. I love singing, so I joined an a capella group, where I made my best friends at UCB.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See the redwoods in Marin, go on trips (you can rent free kayaks at the marina, for example).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Never got used to the water tasting like chlorine though.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: JOIN A CLUB or live in a co op or both, ideally.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The substance culture (ketamine, cocaine, mdma, alcohol, vapes, weed, etc.). People in Berkeley are not heavy drinkers like in Denmark but rather use a lot of other different types of substances. However, most Berkeley students are very open to talk about substances and are generally more vocal about consent than in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and focus on inclusivity (especially in the co ops)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) live in the co ops
2) join a club
3) apply for funding (legater)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I've said it all already

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making friends!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting funding, until I got it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Nope.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
